In [[geometry]], a set of [[line (geometry)|line]]s is called '''equiangular''' if all the lines intersect at a single point, and every pair of lines makes the same angle.

== Equiangular lines in Euclidean space ==
Computing the maximum number of equiangular lines in ''n''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is a difficult problem, and unsolved in general, though bounds are known. The maximal number of equiangular lines in 2-dimensional Euclidean space is 3: we can take the lines through opposite vertices of a regular hexagon, each at an angle 120 degrees from the other two. The maximum in 3 dimensions is 6: we can take lines through opposite vertices of an [[icosahedron]]. It is known that the maximum number in any dimension <math>n</math> is less than or equal to <math display="inline">\binom{n+1}{2}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lemmens|first1=P. W. H|last2=Seidel|first2=J. J|date=1973-03-01|title=Equiangular lines|journal=Journal of Algebra|language=en|volume=24|issue=3|pages=494–512|doi=10.1016/0021-8693(73)90123-3|issn=0021-8693|doi-access=free}}</ref> The maximum in dimensions 1 through 16 is listed in the ''[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]'' as follows:

:1, 3, 6, 6, 10, 16, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 36, 40, ... {{OEIS|id=A002853}}.

In particular, the maximum number of equiangular lines in 7 dimensions is 28.  We can obtain these lines as follows.  Take the vector (−3,−3,1,1,1,1,1,1) in <math>\mathbb{R}^8</math>, and form all 28 vectors obtained by permuting its components.  The [[dot product]] of two of these vectors equals 8 if both have a component of -3 in the same place, and it equals −8 otherwise.  Thus, the lines through the origin containing these vectors are equiangular.  Moreover, all 28 vectors are orthogonal to the vector (1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1) in <math> \mathbb{R}^8</math>, so they lie in a 7-dimensional space.  In fact, these 28 vectors and their negatives are, up to rotation and dilatation, the 56 vertices of the [[3 21 polytope|3<sub>21</sub> polytope]].  In other words, they are the weight vectors of the 56-dimensional representation of the Lie group [[E7 (mathematics)|E<sub>7</sub>]].

Equiangular lines are equivalent to [[two-graph]]s.  Given a set of equiangular lines, let ''c'' be the [[cosine]] of the common angle.  We assume that the angle is not 90°, since that case is trivial (i.e., not interesting, because the lines are just coordinate axes); thus, ''c'' is nonzero.  We may move the lines so they all pass through the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]] of coordinates.  Choose one [[unit vector]] in each line.  Form the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] ''M'' of [[inner product]]s.  This matrix has 1 on the diagonal and ±c everywhere else, and it is symmetric.  Subtracting the [[identity matrix]] ''I'' and dividing by ''c'', we have a [[symmetric matrix]] with zero diagonal and ±1 off the diagonal.  This is the [[Seidel adjacency matrix]] of a two-graph. Conversely, every two-graph can be represented as a set of equiangular lines.<ref>{{harvnb|van Lint|Seidel|1966}}</ref>

The problem of determining the maximum number of equiangular lines with a fixed angle in sufficiently high dimensions was solved by Jiang, Tidor, Yao, Zhang, and Zhao.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Zilin|last2=Tidor|first2=Jonathan|last3=Yao|first3=Yuan|last4=Zhang|first4=Shengtong|last5=Zhao|first5=Yufei|title=Equiangular lines with a fixed angle|journal=Annals of Mathematics|year=2021|volume=194|issue=3|pages=729–743|doi=10.4007/annals.2021.194.3.3|arxiv=1907.12466|s2cid=198967748}}</ref> The answer is expressed in spectral graph theoretic terms. Let <math>N_\alpha(d)</math> denote the maximum number of lines through the origin in <math>d</math> dimensions with common pairwise angle <math>\arccos\alpha</math>. Let <math>k</math> denote the minimum number (if it exists) of vertices in a graph whose adjacency matrix has [[spectral radius]] exactly <math>(1-\alpha)/(2\alpha)</math>. If <math>k</math> is finite, then <math>N_\alpha(d) = \lfloor k(d-1)/(k-1) \rfloor</math> for all sufficiently large dimensions <math>d</math> (here the "sufficiently large" may depend on <math>\alpha</math>). If no <math>k</math> exists, then <math>N_\alpha(d) = d+ o(d)</math>.

== Equiangular lines in complex vector space ==
In a complex [[vector space]] equipped with an [[Inner product space|inner product]], we can define the angle between unit vectors <math>\hat{a}</math> and <math>\hat{b}</math> by the relation <math>\cos(\theta)=|(\hat{a},\hat{b})|</math>. It is known that an upper bound for the number of complex equiangular lines in any dimension <math>n</math> is <math>n^2</math>. Unlike the real case described above, it is possible that this bound is attained in every dimension <math>n</math>. The conjecture that this holds true was proposed by Zauner<ref>{{cite thesis|last=Zauner|first=Gerhard|title=Quantum Designs Foundations of noncommutative Design Theory|date=1999|publisher=University of Vienna|url=http://www.gerhardzauner.at/documents/gz-quantumdesigns.pdf|type=PhD}}</ref> and verified analytically or numerically up to <math>n = 67</math> by Scott and Grassl.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2010-04-01|title=Symmetric informationally complete positive-operator-valued measures: A new computer study|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics|volume=51|issue=4|pages=042203|doi=10.1063/1.3374022|issn=0022-2488|bibcode=2010JMP....51d2203S|last1=Scott|first1=A. J.|last2=Grassl|first2=M.|arxiv=0910.5784|s2cid=115159554}}</ref> A maximal set of complex equiangular lines is also known as a SIC or [[SIC-POVM]].

==Notes==

* J. J. Seidel "Discrete non-Euclidean geometry" In Buekenhout (ed.), ''Handbook of Incidence Geometry'', Elsevier, Amsterdam, The Nederlands (1995) claims, without proof, that the maximum number of equiangular lines in dimension 14 is 28. This was not known at the time.
